HTML comment carrying a system/assistant directive inside fetched resource content (resource content poisoning); not scored offline (resource_content target).
<IMPORTANT>/<SYSTEM> block instructing the agent to read ~/.ssh/id_rsa or cloud credentials.

Description that overrides behaviour of tools served by other MCP servers.

The cited sample returns this notice from tool execution (the tool's docstring stays ordinary PubMed documentation), so it demonstrates the redirect goal at the tool-result layer. This signature covers the description-level variant of the same pattern: an Important-tagged notice that retires the tool, routes calls to another tool and conceals the change; it does not claim to detect the execution-time return value.
A messaging tool description that swaps the real recipient for a proxy phone number (WhatsApp MCP exploit).
Description that forces every transfer to a fixed proxy address and says the user must not be notified (puppet attack).
A standing rule in an unrelated tool that rewrites the recipient of a later send_email call to a fixed address (parameter tampering).

The cited npm campaign hid the blind copy in the email handler's code (a hardcoded Bcc property), not in the tool description, so the attack itself is an implementation backdoor outside the reach of a description scanner. This signature covers the description-level variant of the same goal (a tool that admits or hides a silent blind copy to a fixed external address) and is a hypothetical analogue, not a detection of the disclosed server.
Taxonomy scenario where sensitive data is encoded into DNS subdomain queries against an attacker nameserver.
Description claiming background clipboard, screen or keystroke capture streamed to an external endpoint.
Tool description coaxes the agent into reading a credential file and storing it in one of the tool's own parameters.

Snyk Labs demonstrates a tool-poisoning pattern where hidden instructions tell the agent to read a local settings file (for example a CLI settings.json holding a GitHub token) and send the token to an external URL. This signature covers the description-level directive with or without explicit concealment wording.
Ordinary-looking tool claims a security precondition that makes the agent read a private key file before every call.
Description tells the model to gather environment secrets by name or via os.environ and place the values in a tool argument.
Description tells the model to plant an SSH key or a reverse-shell line in authorized_keys or a shell rc file for persistence.
Post-approval 'upgrade' description that makes the agent read a credentials resource and keep quiet about it.
